# Replaced Belts and They Still Squeak

Replacing serpentine belts on a 2011 Hyundai Elantra is a standard maintenance task, yet the persistent squealing noise when engaging the HVAC system points to a specific mechanical fault unrelated to the belt itself. If you have already verified that the new belts are installed correctly and are not slipping, the issue likely lies in the tensioner assembly or the idler pulleys driving the accessory components.

When the heat is turned on, the engine control module (ECM) commands the A/C compressor clutch to engage. This sudden increase in load requires the serpentine belt to transmit significantly more torque. If the belt squeals only under this specific condition, it indicates that the system cannot handle the immediate spike in tension required by the compressor. The most probable culprit is a failing automatic belt tensioner. Over time, the internal spring within the tensioner weakens, or the pivot bearing develops excessive play. When the compressor kicks in, the tension drops momentarily below the threshold needed to prevent slip, resulting in that high-pitched squeal until the system stabilizes.

To diagnose this without disassembly, observe the behavior of the tensioner arm while the engine is idling and the A/C is off. Apply moderate pressure to the arm with a long screwdriver or pry bar. If you feel significant lateral play (more than 1/4 inch) or hear a clicking sound from the pivot point, the tensioner is worn out. Once the A/C engages, repeat this check. If the play increases noticeably when the compressor loads the system, the tensioner is definitely the source of the noise. Replacing the tensioner is often the most effective solution, as it restores the constant clamping force required to maintain belt integrity under varying load conditions.

However, replacing the tensioner alone is not always a complete fix. The squeal can also stem from worn idler pulleys or a failing compressor bearing. If the compressor bearings are dry or damaged, they create significant friction against the belt. When the A/C engages, this friction causes the belt to slip even if the tensioner is perfectly functional. In these cases, inspecting the pulleys for roughness or wobble is essential. You can spin each pulley by hand; any grinding, clicking, or uneven rotation indicates internal bearing failure.

Another common oversight involves the condition of the new belts themselves. Even brand-new belts can squeak if they are contaminated with oil or coolant residue from a previous leak in the engine block or valve cover gaskets. Oil on the belt surface drastically reduces friction coefficients, leading to slip under load. Before condemning a new belt for noise, ensure the entire accessory drive area is clean and dry. If contamination is found, cleaning the belt and surrounding components with an appropriate solvent is necessary before reassembly.

In some scenarios, replacing the compressor itself is required if the bearings are shot or if the clutch mechanism is dragging. This is a more invasive repair involving coolant drain and potentially removing other accessories like the alternator to gain access. The trade-off between cost and labor must be weighed; sometimes rebuilding the tensioner with a new bearing kit offers a cheaper alternative, though OEM replacements are often preferred for reliability. If the squeal persists after addressing the tensioner, pulleys, and belt condition, it is highly probable that the compressor is the root cause of the noise.
